# Literature Review: CO₂ Emissions and Economic Growth

* Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) Hypothesis:
- Copeland (1995) and Stern (2000) posit an inverted-U relationship: industrialization drives emissions upward; subsequent decarbonization technologies, service-sector transition, institutional reforms reverse trajectory.

* Empirical Evidence:
- Griggs & Davis (1991); Ehsani & Mahmood (2017): cross-sectional panel studies confirm nonlinear emissions-growth nexus across OECD economies.
- Li (2009); Wang et al. (2012): emerging-market analyses reveal threshold effects—emissions peak between per-capita income of $15,000–$20,000.

* Emissions Intensity vs. Absolute Emissions:
- Acemoglu & Restrepo (2011) distinguish intensity-driven decarbonization from absolute emissions reduction; expansion can decouple the two.
- Aghion, Bolton & Ploegh (2017) model technology spillovers in developing economies; R&D-driven green innovation accelerates post-peak decarbonization.

* Policy & Institutional Context:
- Acemoglu, Johnson & Robinson (2005): weak institutions amplify emissions per GDP unit.
- Lintner (2005): carbon-tax implementation reduces emissions 1–4% per dollar, varying by industrial composition.

* Recent Developments:
- Bouffia et al. (2022); Natarajan (2023): post-2020 literature incorporates climate feedbacks, geopolitical shocks, transition risk into growth-emissions models.
- Pierri et al. (2021): digitalization, AI-driven energy optimization may flatten or steepen EKC depending on deployment speed.

* Theoretical Debates:
- Acemoglu & Ploegh (2018) vs. Høyer (2001): green innovation as separate growth engine versus byproduct of income effects.
- Gore (2018): heterodox perspectives reject EKC framework, arguing decoupling remains structurally impossible without radical demand-side transformation.
